newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic, finally, president of Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic, finally, president of Yugoslavia.

text.p: Slobodan Milosevic, once viewed in the West as the uncompromising and bloody champion of resurgent nationalism in Europe, crowned his success as peacemaker by becoming president of Yugoslavia on Wednesday.

Widely blamed around the world for orchestrating Serb separatist attacks in both Croatia and subsequently Bosnia, the pudgy 55-year-old former communist has with a mixture of demagoguery, charm and menacing political skill fulfilled his dream of ruling the Balkan federation.

His switch to the Yugoslav presidency, hitherto a relatively unimportant post, is widely interpreted in Serbia itself as a tactic to remain the political supremo in Belgrade and power broker in the crisis-ridden Balkans.

Yugoslavia has not become the "Greater Serbia" he intended. Instead, it has shrunk to an impoverished Serbia and tiny Montenegro after four other republics succeeded in breaking away despite the best efforts of his generals to crush independence in Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia.

Not long ago Yugoslavia led the non-aligned world, its sophistication and economic development evidence that communism and capitalism could co-exist despite the Cold War. It was a matter of pride that a Yugoslav passport-holder could travel practically anywhere without a visa.
The old-style communist boss with the jutting jaw and steel-coloured hair quickly found his true vocation as the leading apostle of a "Greater Serbia".
He first tried to keep the Yugoslav federation together, and when that failed, tried to mediate its break-up on Serbia's own terms.
Nevertheless he convinced many of his 10 million compatriots the rest of the world was wrong and he was right -- all they had to do was stick together as Serbs, as Slavs and as Orthodox Christians.
Taking office as Serbian president in 1987, he won popularity by cracking down on Kosovo, a province many Serbians regard as the cradle of of their culture despite its ethnic Albanian majority.

Foreseeing the movements for independence of Yugoslavia's other republics, Milosevic prepared the Serbian-led Yugoslav federal army (JNA) while whipping up sectarian feelings at mass rallies in 1988 and 1989.
He changed the constitution to impose direct Serbian rule on the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, removing the autonomy of ethnic Albanians and Hungarians at a stroke.

When Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, Milosevic was ready. The JNA, alongside local Serb militias, fought initially to safeguard Serb minorities but the wars quickly became a vicious grab for territory.

At the end of the day, Serbs held large tracts of Croatia and Bosnia-- some of which they had to give up under the terms of the U.S. brokered Dayton accords in which Milosevic played a prominent role.

Discarding nationalism under pressure of U.N. sanctions which sapped Serbia's economy, in 1995 Milosevic persuaded Bosnian Serb leaders, including indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, to let him represent them in the Dayton talks.
Once branded a war criminal, Milosevic managed to reverse his role to that of peacemaker -- taking on the war lobbies in Serbia and Bosnia he had helped create.
In the process, Milosevic managed to survive the loss of the Krajina enclave in Croatia, the symbol of the dream of Greater Serbia, and a chunk of Bosnia.

Last year he survived a domestic challenge to his authority when an opposition coalition mounted daily protests for three months, rallying up to 500,000 people at the peak of a campaign against local election fraud.
Burly and charming, Milosevic was born in Pozarevac southeast of Belgrade in 1941, the son of a theology teacher.
A lawyer by training, Milosevic is believed to be heavily influenced by his wife, Mirjana, a Belgrade University sociology lecturer and a neo-communist. They have a son and a daughter.
He rarely gives interviews or appears in public, preferring to attend to his popularity among many Serbs, for whom and despite everything he is still the outstanding figure of his time.
